newsitem.title: USA: Albright says U.S. seeks to aid Palestinians despite concerns.
newsitem.headline: Albright says U.S. seeks to aid Palestinians despite concerns.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday she was working to renew U.S. aid to Palestinians despite the bombing of a Jewish market and continued concerns about Yasser Arafat's commitment to Israel's security.

While Arafat assured her by telephone soon after the bombing that he was committed to ensuring a secure environment for the Jewish state, Albright said "we are stressing over and over again that it is important to get the security situation dealt with, that Arafat must do more."

Nevertheless, she said, administration officials were negotiating with Congress to obtain a short-term extension of a law that allows U.S. aid to Palestinians -- viewed as a critical tool in the peace process -- to continue to flow.
Albright spoke to reporters aboard a U.S. Air Force jet returning her to Washington from an Asian trip. She later briefed reporters again during a layover in Hawaii.

A new U.S. effort to revive deadlocked Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations was thrown into doubt earlier on Wednesday when 15 people were blown apart in a packed Jewish market in Jerusalem by two suicide bombers.

Israel halted talks with Arafat and Albright could not suggest when they might be revived or when U.S. Mideast Coordinator Dennis Ross, who was set to take new proposals to the parties later this week, would reschedule his now-delayed trip.

Israeli police said the two Moslem militant bombers, who were among the dead, strolled into the Mahane Yehuda market dressed in jackets and ties with bombs hidden in attache cases. Around 170 people were wounded.
U.S. officials said they understood the bombers may have been dressed up as orthodox Jews.
It was the deadliest attack since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu won election in 1996 vowing to bolster security. The Islamic militant movement Hamas claimed responsibility.
"Clearly the issue of security is paramount," Albright said after airborne telephone calls with Arafat and Netanyahu.

"It is very hard for the peace process to proceed when there is such uncertainty about the security situation. At the same time there is ... an understanding there have to be actions taken on the political front," she said.
"But in the case of Prime Minister Netanyahu understandably his main concern now is security and so that's the gist of the discussions," she said.

The law that makes it possible for the United States to have official dealings with and give aid to Arafat's Palestinian Authority expires on Aug. 12 and there has been doubt about whether Congress will extend it.
Anti-Palestinian sentiment has been rising in Congress as Israeli-Palestinian negotiations over implementing their 1993 peace agreement broke down and violence flared.
Expiration of the Middle East Peace Facilitation Act would end U.S. aid to Palestinians, diplomatic contacts and force the Palestinian Liberation Office to close its Washignton office.

Moreover, even if the law is extended, aid and contacts might have to be cut off temporarily because the administration could not issue the required cerification that Palestinians are complying with obligations under the Oslo peace agreements.

"We're working with the (Capitol) Hill in an effort to try to get an extension on this" but even if it is approved, "at this stage we do not have all the information necessary for the certification process to go forward," Albright said.

She said Washington was seeking more information on Arafat's promise to prosecute four Palestinian police officers arrested recently by Israeli police for apparently plotting a terrorist strike against Israel.
The United States has provided $260 million of a five-year commitment of $500 million to the Palestinians.
Albright bridled at suggestions that because she has not visited the Middle East since taking office six months ago, she has not been sufficiently involved in peacemaking there.

"I am directly involved. Let us make this clear. I have been since the day I became secretary of state," meeting with Middle East leaders on visits to Washington and talking to them on the telephone, she said, adding: "You do not have to be in the region to be personally involved."
